claims.claim: RACI conventions (exactly one accountable, at least one responsible, consulted before, informed after) and the glossary fields listed are common practice.
claims.source: General governance practice, not a quotation from a standard.

concept_html:
Lesson E2-L3 named who decides. A RACI turns that into a table people can check, and a business glossary records what they decided.

RACI. Rows are activities, columns are roles, and each cell holds one letter:

  • R, responsible: does the work. At least one per activity.
  • A, accountable: owns the outcome and signs it off. Exactly one per activity.
  • C, consulted: asked before the decision, a two-way conversation.
  • I, informed: told after it, one way.

Two common failures: an activity with two As, so each waits for the other, and one with no A, so nobody signs off. Name roles, not people, so the table survives a reorganisation.

Business glossary. One entry per business term, such as "active employee" or "regretted leaver". Each entry holds:

  • the term and a plain definition;
  • the calculation rule, where it is a measure, such as which contract types count;
  • the owner (the A for its definition) and the steward who maintains it;
  • the system of record that holds the data;
  • related terms and the ones it must not be confused with;
  • a status (draft or approved), a version and the date approved.

A definition changes only through the escalation path in lesson E2-L3, and every change gets a new version, so a report can say which definition it used.

DMBOK2 places the business glossary in metadata management. Start with the 15 terms that appear most in people reports, not the whole vocabulary.

exercises.prompt_html:
Write raci_problems(raci: dict[str, dict[str, str]]) -> list[str]. raci maps each activity to a dict of role to letter.

Return a sorted list of problems, using exactly these messages:

  • "<activity>: no accountable role" when no role has "A";
  • "<activity>: <n> accountable roles" when more than one has "A";
  • "<activity>: no responsible role" when no role has "R";
  • "<activity>: unknown letter <x> for <role>" for any letter other than R, A, C or I.

Return an empty list when every activity is sound.
solution_lines: VALID_LETTERS = frozenset({"R", "A", "C", "I"})
def raci_problems(raci: dict[str, dict[str, str]]) -> list[str]:
"""Problems in a RACI: missing or duplicate accountable roles, no responsible role, bad letters.
Args:
raci: Activity to a dict of role to letter.
Returns:
The problems found, sorted. Empty when the RACI is sound.
"""
problems: list[str] = []
for activity, cells in raci.items():
letters = list(cells.values())
accountable = letters.count("A")
if accountable == 0:
problems.append(f"{activity}: no accountable role")
elif accountable > 1:
problems.append(f"{activity}: {accountable} accountable roles")
if letters.count("R") == 0:
problems.append(f"{activity}: no responsible role")
for role, letter in cells.items():
if letter not in VALID_LETTERS:
problems.append(f"{activity}: unknown letter {letter} for {role}")
return sorted(problems)

title: A RACI and a business glossary for talent data
why_html: Two HR directors each believed they owned the definition of "headcount", and the RACI listed both as accountable. Each approved a different version for their own reports, so the board pack showed two headcounts 4% apart. Making one of them accountable, and recording the approved definition in the glossary with a version, ended it.
